summary: Defines criteria for designing autonomous system border routers that run BGP with external peers and OSPF as their interior routing protocol. It was replaced by RFC 1403.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router sits on the edge of a network and speaks two routing languages, this document explains how it should translate between them.

how to exchange routes between bgp and ospf
subtitle: How to coordinate BGP and OSPF routing at an AS boundary router

tldr.problem: Large networks often use OSPF inside an autonomous system (AS) and BGP to talk to external networks. A router at the AS boundary must translate routes between the two protocols, but the protocols carry different information in incompatible formats.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines rules for ASBRs: which routes to export from OSPF to BGP and which to import from BGP to OSPF, how to use a 32-bit tag field to carry route characteristics, and how to set BGP attributes like ORIGIN and AS_PATH based on the route source and path information.
tldr.outcome: ASBRs can now reliably exchange routes between OSPF and BGP without losing critical information. However, this RFC was replaced by RFC 1403, which provided updated guidance.

facts.value: Automatic (1), Completeness (1), PathLength (2), ArbitraryTag (12), AutonomousSystem (16) bits

today: RFC 1364 specified BGP and OSPF interaction but is now obsolete. It was replaced by RFC 1403, which provides updated guidance for ASBR configuration.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When a large network uses OSPF as its interior routing protocol (IGP) and BGP for routing to external networks, the routers at the network boundary must run both protocols. These routers are called Autonomous System Border Routers (ASBRs).

The challenge is that OSPF and BGP express routing information differently. OSPF uses costs and metric types; BGP uses a path of autonomous systems and origin information. RFC 1364 defines the rules for how an ASBR should exchange routes between the two protocols, ensuring that important information is not lost and that routes are advertised correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router is on the boundary between your network and the rest of the Internet, it must translate between your internal routing protocol and the external one. This document explains how to do that translation correctly.

sections.title: Route Exchange Between OSPF and BGP
sections.content:
The RFC establishes several key principles. By default, no routes are exported from OSPF into BGP unless explicitly configured. When exporting OSPF routes to BGP, an ASBR must be able to filter at the granularity of a single network and based on OSPF tag values. When a route becomes unreachable via OSPF, the ASBR must immediately propagate that information to external BGP neighbors.

For importing routes from BGP back into OSPF, the principles are even more restrictive. By default, no routes are imported from BGP into OSPF. Routes learned via internal BGP (IBGP) must never be imported into OSPF. The ASBR administrator must explicitly configure each route to import and may need to control whether default routes are originated into the OSPF domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The default is to keep internal and external routes separate. Administrators must explicitly decide which routes to share between the two protocols, to prevent accidentally advertising internal routes or believing external routes too quickly.

sections.title: Identifiers and Router IDs
sections.content:
A critical requirement is that the BGP Identifier must match the OSPF Router ID at all times the router is running. This ensures that if multiple ASBRs in an autonomous system advertise the same external route, other routers and ASBRs can correctly identify which ASBR is the source.

The RFC explains a scenario with three routers: two ASBRs importing external routes into OSPF, and one internal router advertising those routes to other external AS. The internal router uses the OSPF Router ID to determine which ASBR learned the route, and then uses that ASBR's BGP Identifier and AS_PATH to forward packets correctly. Matching the identifiers ensures this mapping is unambiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router has a name. The boundary router must use the same name in both its internal and external routing protocols, so other routers can tell which boundary router a route came from.

sections.title: The OSPF Tag Mechanism
sections.content:
OSPF includes a 32-bit external route tag field that administrators can use to carry information between ASBRs. RFC 1364 specifies how to use this tag to encode route characteristics, so that other routers in the OSPF domain can determine the route's origin and BGP attributes without waiting for BGP updates.

The tag has two modes. In automatic mode (high bit set to 1), the tag encodes four fields: an Automatic bit (set automatically by a router), a Completeness bit (whether the path information is known), a 2-bit PathLength field, a 12-bit ArbitraryTag, and a 16-bit AutonomousSystem number. In manual mode (high bit set to 0), the tag is a 31-bit LocalInfo field configured by the administrator. This dual-mode design allows flexible encoding of route information while maintaining backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the tag as a sticky note on a route. The ASBR writes information on the note saying where the route came from and how reliable that source is. Other routers read the note to decide whether to trust the route.

sections.title: Practical Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC requires that implementations provide mechanisms for administrators to control route exchange with high granularity. For OSPF-to-BGP export, administrators must be able to filter by network, by OSPF tag, and by tag sub-fields. For BGP-to-OSPF import, administrators must configure individual routes or route sets, and optionally configure default route origination based on tuples of network, AS_PATH, cost, and metric type.

A key consideration is timing: the ASBR must propagate route changes quickly from OSPF to BGP neighbors, while also supporting mechanisms to dampen rapid fluctuations (flapping) in route advertisements. Implementations must support minimum delay timers between learning a route via OSPF and advertising it via BGP to external peers.
sections.plainLanguage: Deploying this requires careful configuration. Administrators must decide which routes flow in which direction, and set parameters to prevent instability when routes change rapidly.
